title: Why We High-Five the Winner
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This essay explores why people physically celebrate the successes of others — high-fives, fist bumps, chest bumps — using the psychological concept of 'Basking in Reflected Glory' to explain the phenomenon among passionate fans and colleagues. It notes physical gestures of celebration reinforce a sense of shared community achievement and can genuinely boost a supporter's self-esteem and identity. The piece draws a clear line, however, between healthy shared celebration and the more problematic instinct to actively seek personal credit for someone else's success, closing with the recommendation to keep the celebratory instinct but drop any claim to borrowed credit.
points: Names 'Basking in Reflected Glory' as the psychological mechanism behind physically celebrating others' wins.
Argues physical celebration gestures genuinely strengthen community bonds and can boost a supporter's own self-esteem and identity.
Distinguishes healthy shared celebration from an unhealthy escalation into actively seeking personal credit for someone else's achievement.
Notes workplace celebration is typically more restrained than sports fandom but follows the same underlying psychological pattern.
Closes with a clear behavioral prescription: keep celebrating others genuinely, but never seek credit for successes you had no real role in.
quotes: Whatever the reason, spectators, fans, and colleagues like to physically acknowledge achievement. To share in the celebration, they hand-slap, high-five, fist pump, and chest bump with the winner or champion.

The association they feel with the champion is galvanized by the physical display. The physical reinforcement brings the champion and those who support them closer together, fostering a sense of community achievement that both share.
In more extreme cases of identification, psychologists refer to this phenomenon as “Basking in Reflected Glory.” It is especially prevalent among the most passionate and devoted fans and supporters.
But when the identification with the achiever is heightened, spectators or colleagues can sometimes seek credit from peers and leaders for the winner’s success.
But building self-esteem from the victories of others is a bridge too far. It is better for you to create your own success than to live vicariously through the victories of others.
